newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Prospects grow for an international criminal court.
newsitem.headline: Prospects grow for an international criminal court.

text.p: Prospects for the establishment of an international criminal court received a major boost on Friday when a U.N. committee decided a conference would be held in 1998 to complete and adopt a convention setting up such a tribunal.
A resolution adopted without a vote by the General Assembly's legal committee also decided that an existing preparatory committee would hold three sessions in 1997 and one in early 1998.

After that, a "diplomatic conference of plenipotentiaries will be held in 1998, with a view to finalising and adopting a convention on the establishment of an international criminal court," the resolution said. Italy has already offered to host the conference.

Such a court would be able to try individuals for gross breaches of international humanitarian law, such as genocide and other serious crimes, although the list of offences to come under its jurisdiction is one of the issues still to be decided.

An international criminal court would differ from the 15-judge World Court at The Hague, formally known as the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945 as the principal judicial arm of the United Nations. It does not try individuals but rules on legal disputes between governments and delivers advisory opinions at the request of U.N. bodies.
Work on an international criminal court has been continuing for several years.

In 1994, the Geneva-based U.N. International Law Commission completed a draft statute, or set of rules, for such a tribunal. This provided the basis for further discussion by a special U.N. committee in 1995 and by a preparatory committee set up last December that held two sessions this year.

The idea of an international criminal court received growing support when, in the absence of such a tribunal, the U.N. Security Council set up two separate courts, in 1993 and 1994, to deal with war crimes in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda.

Before the Assembly's legal committee adopted Friday's resolution by consensus, Carolyn Willson of the United States said she fully supported it but was unable to participate in the decision because it was not certain that six weeks' work by the the preparatory committee in 1997 could be financed out of existing U.N. resources.

The United States would try to ensure those meetings would be serviced without additional costs and hoped to join in the consensus when the resolution came before the General Assembly plenary for endorsement.

Among issues still to be decided are the relationship between the proposed court and the U.N. Security Council, where the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France have permanent seats and a veto. Also to be resolved is how the tribunal would complement national courts and whether it should deal with such crimes as international terrorism, drug trafficking and attacks against U.N. personnel.
